subtopic: AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, in Toronto, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture is meeting to prepare an action plan in response to the Mulroney-Wilson Budget which has betrayed Canadian farmers. In a statement made on June 6, the OFA said:
The Government has not only ignored its own promises, it has ignored the legitimate needs of our farmers.
Ontario farmers are angry because the Budget did nothing to ease the debt burden hanging over many farmers which, in counties like Bruce, has reached epidemic proportions so that one in three farmers is in serious financial difficulty.
At the same time the Government is increasing farm input costs. For example, it will impose a nine-cent per gallon excise tax on farm fuels on the first of September, just in time for the fall harvest. Imagine a Government so arrogant, so insensitive, so uncaring of the plight of farmers, that it imposes a harvest tax on Canadian agriculture.
In January the Government will impose an additional 1 per cent sales tax on all farm input costs of equipment and supplies. It will also reduce Department of Agriculture programs by $50 million a year.
No wonder the OFA is considering plans today for drastic action, like mass demonstrations, withholding FCC payments, and rotating food strikes. Only strong measures such as these will make the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) understand the serious plight of Canadian farmers.

subtopic: DISASTERS
DISASTERS
subsubtopic: WORKERS' MEMORIAL DAY-ANNIVERSARY OF SUDBURY MINING TRAGEDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20, 1984, a rockburst occurred at the No. 5 shaft of the Falconbridge mine. This rockburst cost four men-Sulo Korpela, Daniel Lavalle, Wayne St. Michel, and Richard Chenier- their lives, and was the largest mining disaster in Sudbury's recent history. These workers were members of Local 598 of the Mine Mill and Smelter Workers' Union.
I am informing the House that tomorrow, June 20, is the first Workers' Memorial Day, organized by the trade union movement in the Sudbury Basin. It is being held one year to the day after the tragic rockburst which claimed the lives of these four miners. However, this Memorial Day goes beyond that tragic incident and remembers all workers in Canada who have lost their lives on the job. Moreover, tomorrow's remembrance is a tribute to workers everywhere who are the foundation upon which our society is built.
Statistics show that one Canadian worker is injured on the job every 16 seconds, and that occupational accidents and diseases are the third leading cause of death. Indeed, workplace and work related diseases kill more than 900 Canadian workers every year.
It is time to pause and reflect upon the valued contribution workers make to our society. We must never forget the risks inherent in this contribution.

subtopic: POLITICAL PARTIES
POLITICAL PARTIES
subsubtopic: PENSIONS-POSITION TAKEN BY LIBERAL PARTY AND NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last two weeks the Liberal Party and the NDP have been acting out a political farce on the floor of the House of Commons. That would be bad enough at any time, but these two Parties have made the old age pensioners of Canada the goats in their performance, and that is inexcusable.
It is fair ball to argue facts, but opposition Members have been using their imagination in arriving at figures far into the future which are actually ridiculous, as well as words that are false. Day after day they have been asking the Government to restore and reinstate the indexing of old age pensions. They know that we cannot restore something that has not been taken away. Then, to frighten the aged further, they move their strawman calculations into the nineties, and weep crocodile tears over the millions which they kid themselves will be taken from the pockets of pensioners in 1991.
There is no Bill before the House to take away any of the indexing from pensioners. There has not been one cent taken off their cheques or their pensions.
Why are the socialists and their spouse, the Liberals, acting like intoxicated drug addicts? I will tell the House why. The Liberal Party and the NDP do not like the proper plan of the Government to remove the indexing from the pay-cheques of MPs and Senators, and they are using the pensioners as a back-door way to save their own indexing. Worse than that, the Liberal Party and the NDP are trying to build their political machines on the backs of the aged, and I say: "Shame".

[ Translation]

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RESPECT ITS PLEDGES
speechtext:
Last week and again yesterday, Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and I toured Quebec ridings represented by Progressive Conservative Members to find out whether there is any truth in what the Prime Minister and his colleagues have been saying. THE ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: CANADIAN EGG MARKETING AGENCY DENIAL OF PRODUCTION QUOTA TO NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
CANADIAN EGG MARKETING AGENCY DENIAL OF PRODUCTION QUOTA TO NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency is best known to Canadians as that organization which has destroyed millions of eggs in order to keep consumer prices high. Now CEMA has hit a new low. It has denied the Northwest Territories access and a requested minimum quota of 200,000 layers.
Apparently the colonialist mentality of CEMA is such that it would oblige the Territories to import vast quantities of food from the south, but will not allow them to export one of the few agricultural commodities which might be competitively produced in the north, in return. At the same time as it sanctions the importation of millions of dollars worth of eggs into Canada from the United States, CEMA refuses the
June 19, 1985

creation of jobs in the Northwest Territories and the employment of Canadians to produce eggs needed by Canadian families.
If this is to be the attitude of CEMA, then I say let us get rid of it and let us have a fair, open, and competitive marketplace from which both producers and consumers can benefit.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS
SMALL BUSINESS
subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL COMMITMENT TO HELP DEVELOP SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for those of us who have been small-businessmen, and those of us who are concerned with such entrepreneurs, we recognize full well the onerous regulations and paper burdens which in the past have been placed on our small-businessmen. These burdens have not been without cost to a large number of small businesses which are struggling to develop a lucrative Canadian business.
I am pleased to see that this problem has been recognized and corrective measures have been initiated with the Intergovernmental Position Paper on The Principles and Framework for Regional Economic Development. This document, which was fully endorsed by all Governments, reflects a commitment to develop more effective policies for small and medium sized businesses. A reduction in the regulatory and paper burdens placed on small businesses is a positive step which will undoubtedly benefit all of the 750,000 Canadian small businesses.

subtopic: PENSIONS
PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about a constituent from Scarborough Centre. She is a widow. In August she will be 75 years old. She is a Canadian by choice, and fiercely proud of it. During the Depression she and her husband worked to build a life. He went to war and was severely wounded, and she still receives a small pension from the Department of Veterans Affairs. They worked hard to obtain their dream, a home. However, in 1967 her husband died suddenly. Working as a mail clerk she paid off her small mortgage, and continued to do volunteer work in the community.
This 74-year old lady pays for food for herself and her two companions, cats. She pays property taxes, electricity and water bills, and telephone bills.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) talks about deficits. Yet he gives billions of dollars to rich investors, speculators,
Oral Questions
and oil companies. The 74-year old lady in Scarborough Centre talks about nickels and dimes and how the deindexation of her pension will hurt. I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to prevail upon the Minister of Finance and ask him to rise today to admit that he has made a mistake, and that he will reintroduce in the Chamber today full pensions for all senior citizens from coast to coast.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: When the committee adjourned at nine o'clock p.m. yesterday, Clause 2 of the Bill and the amendment of the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) were under consideration.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the subject matter of the amendment before the House today has been the subject matter of Question Period for some time now. That subject matter today prompted an Hon. Member to say words, the saying of which caused him to be removed from the House of Commons. The main reason that this subject matter has been before the House for some time and the main reason for the events of today is that Members find it very difficult to understand the reasoning of a Government that promised one thing, reiterated that promise in December, and then reneged on that promise in the Budget.
We have listened to Cabinet Ministers and to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance try to rationalize the cut in the projected increase of old age pensions which is due to take effect on January 1. Today we listened to the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister try to prove that the disposable income of senior citizens will not be affected by all that much. I presume the Parliamentary Secretary, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance were relying on expert advice received from various quarters.
I found it very difficult to understand what the spokesman for the Government was talking about last evening in this Chamber. He said that there was not really a 3 per cent cut. In fact, he said that the disposable income of seniors was only down by 1.5 percentage points. Then, not satisfied with that, he went even further to say that the cut is really only one half of 1.5 per cent. He then tried to justify that by saying that senior citizens could adjust by buying different products or changing their style of living to accommodate the .75 per cent cut.
I am sure that people who were listening to that argument were racking their brains trying to determine what kind of economic reasoning he was using. Perhaps the hon. gentleman was taking advice from experts who were schooled in the days when economics was called political economy. In those days, one observed the fact and then imagined some other facts in order to come to a conclusion which could only be verified over the long term. However, in those days of Plato and Aristotle, ethics was an issue. After that time, the Romans at least talked about the gods as being the final determining point.
What reasoning can be used for this? We can talk about the law of supply and demand, but if the price of coffee goes up too much, people will turn to tea, postum, or hot chocolate. If there were not enough coffee beans in Brazil, we would substitute. But Mr. Chairman, how can that same reasoning be used with regard to the cut of senior citizens' pensions? What kind of substitution is available with regard to flour, one of their basic commodities? If there were any difference between Red Rose flour and Cream of the West flour, it would only be a couple of cents. You cannot go to a different oil company and pay less money for home heating oil. You can change the name of the supplier, but you do not get it any cheaper. You cannot go to another telephone company to get a cheaper telephone or to a different electric company to get
June 19, 1985

cheaper electricity. Contrary to what the Government of Canada is telling senior citizens, they cannot substitute to make up for this particular cut.
The Government says that it received its advice from experts. When the Prime Minister went to his riding to speak last evening, many people believed that he was going to announce that the Government was reversing its position on old age pensions. I believed that if he was going to his riding to make an announcement, it would be that he was finally digging in his heels on behalf of 700 workers in his riding and was going to negotiate with the United States the removal of the incredibly bad tariff on saltfish that affects his riding.
However, neither of those matters were discussed. The Prime Minister announced that the Government of Canada was going to build a maximum security prison in his riding to provide jobs for the people of his riding. Presumably that was also on the advice of the so-called experts, who advise politicians but who do not know reality in the ridings.
1 suppose one could go to any Member's riding and announce the construction of a maximum security prison. I suggest half the constituents would agree and half would not. However, that was the advice of the experts, just as they advised that this measure was not a 3 per cent cut but a cut of 1.5 per cent because senior citizens can adjust, buy cheaper products and change their lifestyle. How can senior citizens change their lifestyle when they must meet mortgages or rent payments, light payments, telephone payments and food payments? It cannot be done.
That is the reason for the motion before the House today. I introduced the motion on the basis that the borrowing authority for which the Government of Canada was asking was not clear in any event. The explanations given by the Minister of State for Finance were inadequate. She did not know what Cabinet Ministers said in response to the President of the Treasury Board since the time that the announced cuts were made in November and one-third of those particular measures taken by the Government were reversed. The Minister of State for Finance could not respond to that question when the Bill was first introduced. Perhaps if she had been able to respond at that time, we would have been able to deal with this Bill much more quickly. However, she could not do so.
Serious questions arise when one examines this borrowing authority Bill in more detail with respect to each Department. These concerns relate to definite figures that were listed by the President of the Treasury Board as savings to the Government of Canada or as revenue from increased fees for the use of federal facilities.
Let me talk about the $200 million that would be saved through extra monitoring regarding the Department of Employment and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I suggest to the Minister of Employment and Immigration that that figure cannot be realistically achieved. She can only reach that goal by introducing many measures that affect many poor people. One step which the
Borrowing Authority Act
Minister probably wants to take is to remove people from unemployment insurance by bringing them into the employment offices. Another probable plan of the Minister is to give these people jobs from government programs that are outlined in the Budget in which funds are allocated to Employment and Immigration for programs under Section 38 or programs being devised together with the provinces. However, there is a danger with respect to direct employment programs under Section 38. A person drawing unemployment insurance who takes a job under the Minister's direct employment program under Section 38 will be taking employment that is not insurable. It is possible that someone entering employment under the Canada Works Program could have his or her payments drop from $260 a week to $200 a week. That would be an injustice to that individual. However, they are mechanisms for lowering the amounts paid out under the unemployment insurance benefits in order to save $200 million.
What are the effects of such action? When the Department of Employment and Immigration announces a work program or an initiative for employment in those parts of Canada with high unemployment, the biggest issue is discrimination. Through its measures, the Government has attempted to put people into existing jobs and take them off unemployment insurance in order to save on unemployment insurance benefits. However, it can only do so if it changes the hiring criteria.
The Government has developed two criteria for employment. Only those drawing unemployment insurance and those who have run out of unemployment insurance benefits can go to work. However, as a result of that action, it is impossible for someone who has never drawn unemployment insurance to get a job under a direct job creation program. In other words, all the young people cannot even get a referral.
The biggest issue facing the Government in areas of high unemployment are these announcements which it makes. Similarly, the Minister of Employment and Immigration stands in the House to talk about the Government's new initiative with respect to the student employment program. While I do not see anything wrong with these jobs going out to private enterprise for the first time, I am concerned when fast food chains in Canada can take advantage of the program. When they would normally hire 30 young people, under this program they will hire 30 young people but have some of their wages subsidized. I am also concerned about these firms hiring people to replace others who would normally take those jobs.
However, let us look at the hiring criteria for this program. First, a candidate must have attended a full time course of instruction during the previous year and must be going to another full time course of instruction. This issue was raised with the Minister some time ago in committee and she said that it would be changed this year. However, it was never changed. Today, there is discrimination in that someone who had not attended a full time course of instruction the previous year, but attended part time instruction and needs that summer job as much as anyone else, is not allowed to get a referral. Someone who only had to complete a few courses is

June 19, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
not allowed to be referred to this summer student employment program.
We come back to the question of experts advising Ministers on hiring criteria. Second, you have experts advising the Ministers on the direction in which the funds will go, and, third, you have experts advising the Ministers on absolute figures relating to cuts that will be included in the Budget and in the financial statement.
I suppose it was the experts who advised the Minister of the Environment to cut out the activities of the Canadian Wildlife Service, Mr. Chairman. I suppose it was the experts who advised the Minister of the Environment that she can charge for every telephone call to the weather office or that she can cut out her guided tours in the national parks this year. I suppose they were the same experts who advised the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on how to do away with the fishing vessel insurance scheme. All of these things have been cancelled as government policy since the financial statement came out in November.
While I am on the subject of employment and immigration, I would like to tell the Minister that in the November financial statement and what is included in the Budget for her Department this year, in the section headed Mobility Grants, there is a cut of about $2.2 million. What happened when that was cut? When that was cut, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, through her officials, had to come out with new guidelines about who qualifies and who does not qualify for mobility grants. What do we see now? In order to get from point A to point B for a person normally qualified for mobility assistance by the Government of Canada, what must happen now? The person has to have a letter saying the job is permanent for over a year. That person also must allow the closest Manpower office to advertise the job for a reasonable period of time. All kinds of restrictions have been imposed. I say to the Minister of Employment and Immigration that she is not only going to save $2.2 million, she is going to save the whole kitty. Nobody will be able to qualify. It will be the exception and not the rule that somebody will receive assistance under that program.
I see, Mr. Chairman, that you are indicating I have only two minutes left and that I have spoken for 18 minutes.

This was never included in the Budget presented to this House and is not included in the Estimates of the Department. It is another subject of great importance to many people in Canada.
Let me conclude by saying that I hope all Members will participate in this debate as it relates to the senior citizens and the trick played on them by this new Government of Canada. Unless this Government reverses itself, it will see a considerable drop in support in the polls in the next election which will be attributable to the senior citizens.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to take part in this debate on Bill C-51 in Committee of the Whole to denounce this Government, which wants to govern by attacking the weakest among us, by taking no action and by increasing the tax burden of low income taxpayers and reducing the income of senior citizens.
On April 2, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Press reported the following comments taken from a study sponsored by the Canada Union of Public Employees, and I quote:

The Conservative Government is deepening an already serious moral disorder in society by popularizing the philosophy of business first. The law of survival of the fittest threatens to reverse the progress that has been made toward a more caring and equitable society.
[ Translation]
Mr. Chairman, the Budget brought down on May 23 lends support to this analysis and also proves that the Mulroney-Wilson alliance has no idea of the real needs of the Canadian economy.

First, by increasing taxes, the Mulroney Government dug deep into the pockets of the ordinary Canadian taxpayer. A married person, earning $20,000 a year, with a spouse and two children, will pay an extra $300 a year as a result of the new Budget. If the same individual earned $30,000 a year, the Budget's bite will be even bigger, in the range of about $400. Second, the temporary surtax on high-income individuals is structured in such a way that it will not hit some of the earners at the higher reaches of the income scale. In fact, since the surtax is based on the tax paid instead of the income itself, it will only hit those Canadians who are unable to reduce their taxable income through special tax deductions. Most high-income individuals will continue to pay little or no tax, but the average Canadian will have to pay much more. Third, the Budget eliminates the full indexation of personal exemptions and tax brackets.
This measure raises taxes for all income groups, but the increase is proportionally larger as a percentage of income for
June 19, 1985

low-income individuals. This change amounts to a tax increase, since it means that as a person's income rises, he or she is pushed into a higher tax bracket and pays more taxes.
[ Translation]
In addition to all these unacceptable measures, the Conservative Government is directly hitting the elderly by reducing the value of Old Age Security Benefits in real dollars. All Canadian men and women over 65 will lose 3 per cent of the value of their pension income this year, if we compare what they will be receiving under the Budget with the amount allocated under the former Liberal Government.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, since the benefits will be indexed only to that part of the cost-of-living increase that is in excess of 3 per cent, in ten years the elderly will lose about 30 per cent of the expected income they would otherwise have had.
For eight weeks last summer during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) travelled across the country promising "jobs, jobs, jobs." Today, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should be shouting "taxes, taxes, taxes."
Unlike the legendary Robin Hood, they are stealing from the poor to give to the rich.
Spending on agriculture has been cut back $15 million annually.
There will be a new federal tax of 11 per cent on health and beauty aids, including soap, toothpaste and so forth.
After dropping its energy conversion programs, the Government has added a new 11 per cent tax on materials used to increase energy effectiveness.
Mr. Speaker, I have been trying to understand how, a Government could bring down a Budget that is so thoroughly unbalanced, and why.
1 have been trying to understand, and so have most of my constituents, who are typical of the middle class that is the backbone of our country.
Unfortunately, the answer is only too obvious.
The biggest hand-out authorized by the Minister of Finance goes to the oil and gas corporations. The corporation hand-out will cost the Treasury $902 million in forgone revenue for the year 1986-87 alone, as a result of eliminating the tax on oil and gas revenue: $902 million in one fiscal year!
Furthermore, the so-called temporary 5 per cent surtax applying to large corporations, a tax the Minister of Finance is very fond of mentioning, will raise $175 million this year and $285 million in 1986-87.
Considering the annual present of $902 million to the oil companies, there is another $440 million that will have to come out of the taxpayers' pockets. How easy it is to increase
Borrowing Authority Act
the gasoline tax by 2 cents a litre, reduce old age security benefits, and cut back job creation programs to recuperate that money. But the Minister of Finance will probably say that Canada's economic recovery will be initiated by the private sector, particularly by small and medium-sized businesses.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance stated in his Budget speech that Canada's small and medium-sized businesses have become the driving force of the Canadian economy. Unfortunately the May 23 Budget does very little to promote that sector of activities and in fact puts our small and medium-sized businesses in a state of stagnation.
Let us review those measures concerning the private sector, beginning with the capital gains tax exemption. Although very few Canadians will be eligible, that kind of measure would have helped small and medium-sized companies if the Government, through carelessness, had not forgotten that the exemption ought to be turned into an investment. As a result of that negligence, very few investors will be attracted by small and medium-sized companies. Since investment in such companies does not provide tax incentives, nobody will want to invest in venture undertakings. Not only will this measure not necessarily create jobs, but it will promote a climate of excessive speculation. The investor will be satisfied since he can sell out to buy a condominium in Florida, but that kind of deal does not create a single job.
Secondly, investment of funds from pension plans and other retirement income schemes in small businesses. This program is regulated through a series of cumbersome and complicated provisions and prevents owners from investing in their own companies.
Like most small business owners, the Liberal Party would have been in favour of investment provisions similar to those now applicable to self-managed retirement saving plans. In that case the owner and his family could have invested in the company thanks to flexible regulations geared to the needs of small investors. The Conservative Government chose to restrict the program to organizations with huge assets, though it knew that generally speaking those organizations stear clear of risky investments. The employees who contribute to this fund to provide for their retirement years will certainly not want huge amounts to be invested in high risk ventures.
Third, we have the issue of research and development. The Budget proposes that the credit acquired by private companies for their current research and development expenditures be 100 per cent refundable. These companies were already able to obtain a refund equal to 40 per cent of their expenditures the first year and to write off the rest of their expenditures over a maximum of seven years.
We believe that, instead of helping the entire job creating sector of small businesses, this proposal will provoke the appearance of companies which will operate only for a short term and be used as a screen for speculators.

June 19, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party of Canada considers it essential to create programs to help young Canadians between 18 and 35 to start their own businesses. In addition, our Party finds it just as important to help Canadian unemployed workers aged between 36 and 55 to use their acquired experience to start their own small businesses.
On the other hand, capital losses should be 100 per cent deductible. We should also promote pension funds specifically aimed at small businessmen. Regulations should be made more flexible and the tax burden of smaller businesses should be reduced.
New means of financing should be created and new markets have to be developed. We believe that it would be possible thus to maintain the rate of growth of smaller businesses and to promote the creation of new job producing businesses, but 1 realize, Mr. Chairman, that the Progressive Conservative Government has decided to reward its closest friends rather than concern itself with creating the jobs which are so badly needed to reduce unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, I should remind you that last month, after eight months of a Progressive Conservative Government, Statistics Canada reported that 10.9 per cent of Canadians were unemployed and that the rate of unemployment for young people under 24 was as high as 17 per cent. Job creation should be a priority for any responsible Government, but the Mulroney-Wilson tandem has found nothing better to do than to increase by about $400 the costs of the average Canadian family.
Instead of "jobs, jobs, jobs", Prime Minister Mulroney should have said during the electoral campaign: "Get ready to be bled white to help fill the pockets of my closest allies!"

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, today in Question Period, I directed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare concerning statements made by a member of the Minister's constituency staff in Provencher, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press. That staff member commented upon the reaction, interest and controversy generated by the Government's move to deindexation by saying:
I think most people don't quite understand how little it is in dollar terms. It means three packs of cigarettes a month that I shouldn't smoke anyway, or half a bottle of liquor that I shouldn't drink.
So where's the hardship?
I asked the Minister twice to repudiate that statement. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is supposed to be the spokesperson in Cabinet who represents the interests of senior citizens, but he refused to comment. He refused to say that his staff member was misquoted. He refused to say that he was wrong. He refused to say that he disagreed with those comments. In other words, he was tacitly agreeing to the comments of his staff member, that there is no hardship, that it means only a half bottle of booze or something. That is the way a member of the Minister's staff is treating the plaintive appeal and cry of hundreds of senior citizens about the hardship which they will have to face. This tells us an awful lot about the Government and its attitude toward this issue, that if it can pawn it off or deny the truth, it will get away with it.
In the same June 17 article, a number of Conservative Members of Parliament are quoted as saying: "It is not an issue in my riding", "I have only had one or two calls", "people don't care", "people are not interested", or "it is simply something which is being hoked up by the Opposition".
Today I presented 4,000 names of residents of the Province of Manitoba. Those were the petitions I received last week. They included close to 2,000 names of residents of Conservative ridings in that province. They were not people who were simply making up things. I see the Hon. Member for St. Boniface in his seat. He said that he had only about 15 calls from his constituents. I have several hundreds of names of constituents from his riding who signed the petition. Something is wrong. Either these constituents are not prepared to tell their Conservative Members of Parliament because they are afraid of them or they know they will not listen, or else Conservative MPs have taken their telephones off the hook. Perhaps the newspapers are simply not telling it as it is.
There is no question that there is a large-scale, incredible demand across this country for a change in this program. What we have instead is a Minister of National Health and Welfare who refuses to even acknowledge that there is a hardship. At the same time, we have a letter from the National Advisory Council on Aging, not a partisan group, not a political group, but made up of representatives of different senior citizens' organizations and social agencies across the country, to advise the Government on its policies. What do they have to say in their statement and in the letter that they wrote to the Minister himself? I would like to quote the following from their letter, which states that, according to the Council:
... "it will provide a short term saving in exchange for a long-term loss". "The stress associated with a tighter and tighter budget will take its toll. More and more senior Canadians will find it difficult to cope with a deteriorating physical, mental and social condition. In time, expenditures for other types of care will limit the savings due to de-indexing".
We have a Minister of National Health and Welfare who denies the evidence, facts and proposals put forward by his own advisory council. He does not even care about them. Instead, he apparently agrees with the staff member who says there is no hardship. That is the problem that we are facing and why this debate is going on. Somehow we have to find a way to penetrate into the conscience of the members of this Conservative caucus and make them understand that this is an issue that cuts to the very heart of this country, that we are talking about something that will substantially alter the social structure of Canada, that we will, for the first time in years, make a deliberate policy choice to force more people into poverty.
Statistics Canada has been reporting, I think, for something like two to three decades. It said in every one of those years that there was a slight improvement, sometimes higher some-
June 19, 1985

times lower, in the number of people coming off the poverty line. It was not always as great as we would have liked, but we have been making steady progress for two decades. It now reports that, for the first time in 20 years, because of this Government's Budget, there will be more Canadians going back below the poverty line, and 250,000 of those will be senior citizens. That is a Statistics Canada report, it is not from a political partisan group. It is reaching a point where we can no longer comprehend what is going on in the inner circles and inner discussions of members of this Conservative caucus when fact after fact is laid on the table that the results of their actions will be to push more people into poverty, it will make it harder for older people in particular to purchase their goods and services . . .

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Blush when you say that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I don't blush at all, Mr. Chairman. I just gave the figures, and this Minister is like his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He is beyond comprehension; he is beyond conscience, he is beyond understanding. He does not understand that for 20 years we have had progress and improvement, and because of the actions of his Government, of which he is a part, we are now going to take a step backwards. That, Mr. Chairman, is a clear sign of the kind of Government we have. It is a Government without a conscience, without understanding, without comprehension.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I don't think they care.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is even beyond not caring. You have to wonder about a Government that deliberately, consciously, takes a decision to put more people into poverty, and then has the Prime Minister stand up day after day, along with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and deny it.
Is it any wonder that the group of senior citizens who mobilized on the front lawn of this Parliament today said, and 1 won't use an unparliamentary expression, that they don't trust this Government anymore, that they don't believe what it says, that they have lost all sense of confidence in anything it stands for? It would be somewhat understandable if it had made a mistake in the Budget. It is a new Government, there are a bunch of rookies in Cabinet, it would be understandable if, maybe in their rush, they went ahead and did things of which they did not perceive the consequences. That is possible. But we had the Minister of National Health and Welfare today in the House standing up and acknowledging, by his approval of the statements of his own staff member, that there will be no hardship. I wonder what kind of reports he is reading. What kind of funny books, what kind of fantasyland is he existing in? It is time for that Minister to be shifted. It is time to try to find somebody in that 211-member caucus who understands the issues. Can you possibly have a Minister of National Health and Welfare who is so incapable, so absolutely obdurate and indifferent to the plight of his constituents that he is not even prepared to say that he was wrong or that his staff member was wrong and, yes, there will be hardships? Mr. Chairman, the evidence is so clear, and it is so obvious.

We are here to say that we have time and time again asked members of this caucus to talk to their Minister, say to him, for goodness' sake there is nothing wrong with acknowledging a mistake. They are now going to lose 3 per cent per year. Inflation has not stopped. If we look at the Consumer Price Index, we see that the cost of food increased this year by an amount in excess of 3 per cent. All items excluding food are up more than 4 per cent. Coming as I do from a prairie community where the cost of energy represents a large expense for senior citizens, we should also look at the effect of inflation there. The aggregate increase in the cost of energy is 7.3 per cent. Transportation costs, which is also of great importance to people who live in small towns and villages and find it necessary to travel to larger centres to visit doctors and obtain health services, have increased more than 5 per cent.
Our senior citizens will face all of these cost increases but their cheques, instead of going up by 3.9 per cent, the full rate of inflation at the moment, will only go up by .9 per cent. Yes, the Government is correct, the cheques will continue to be slightly larger, but they will not buy as much.
I think this issue might have been made more clear if, on the presentation of the Budget, it had been described as a head tax or poll tax. In effect, that is what it is. Seniors are being asked to bear an additional 3 per cent tax per year. If this were billed as a poll tax, the response would have been much more immediate. As it was, seniors waited to look at the Budget themselves and saw that it said "will take place effective January, 1986". They saw those words and understood what they meant. They began sending petitions to their Members of Parliament and we have been presenting those petitions. They have now begun sending delegations to Ottawa, one of which arrived here today.
I would like to spend a few minutes reviewing a few of the things the members of that delegation told us. They spoke very clearly and succinctly. I should explain to the front-benchers opposite some of the values held by our senior citizens. These values are held by all citizens in certain parts of the country, but when I watch the activities of certain Members on the front bench opposite, I see very little evidence of them.
Mrs. Fraser, a retired health services worker from Halifax, told us that there are people in her city suffering stress related diseases which were triggered by worrying about their financial circumstances. Their budgets are very restricted now and they know that their expenses will continue to increase while their Old Age Security pensions will be cut by 3 per cent.
Mrs. Fraser cited three examples, one of a high blood pressure case, one of a heart attack, and another of a problem brought on by intense feelings of insecurity due to worrying about the future. To many younger people, that may not seem possible. However, many older people, who have only their futures to prepare for, take this very seriously. Some of them do not have enough social activities to keep them occupied and worrying becomes an obsession.
Having grown up in the time in which they did, they feel betrayed. During the election campaign they were promised that deindexation would not be pursued by the new Government. Page 60 of the Progressive Conservative Handbook says, "A PC Government would once more index the old age pension to the actual cost of living on a quarterly basis". That is what the seniors expected. On page 11 of the Consultation Paper on Child and Elderly Benefits it says, "In the Government's view no change is required in the OAS-GIS payments system".
Everyone thought that meant that there would be no change, that we would continue to have the automatic indexing of the consumer price index on a quarterly basis, and that pensioners would have that to rely upon. However, that has not happened. That which was portrayed as a sacred trust was only an election platform. It was only meant to sooth anxieties caused prior to Christmas when some front-benchers started to make noises about deindexation and changing social programs. With the presentation of the Budget, we learned that sacred trusts and questions of confidence were no longer that important.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance forget that our senior citizens were raised to believe that a man's word was the most treasured commodity in existence. They saw those words, that trust, and that confidence broken. Their old fashioned values are now very much in question. Senior citizens want to know their pensions are being discounted by 3 per cent annually starting in 1986. They have had no answers. There have been no excuses other than some vague murmur-ings that the country cannot afford it.
The motion which is before the Committee presently proposes the reduction of the borrowing authority by 3 per cent. The Government is asking for $18.2 billion of borrowing authority. Three per cent of that would be approximately $560 million. That is the amount of money that we are asking seniors to give up by the end of 1987. This borrowing authority is over and above that which the Government will collect from Canadians through taxes. This borrowing authority will basically go to increase the deficit. This motion proposes to reduce the borrowing authority by $550 million and to put the onus on the whole country to provide the money that the Govern-
June 19, 1985

Mr. Chairman, I am referring to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. In recent weeks, since the Budget was brought down, we have seen how surprised and disappointed Canadians were at the cavalier, underhanded and insidious way the Prime Minister and his Government accomplices have been trying to conceal tax increases telling the elderly: "Now, we are all friends and we are all one happy family", and then cutting 3 per cent off their pensions while using a lot of complicated words to confuse the issue.

Yesterday, we were challenged right and left with all sorts of figures which I think I have laid to rest. Today, I should like to challenge hon. members of the NDP who support this amendment and oppose this bill. I should like them to try to prove that the Prime Minister was wrong when he stated that 271,000 had been created since September 1984, that 159,000 jobs were created in April and May, the greatest number for a two month period in 12 years, not to mention the fact that unemployment in May had dropped from 10.9 per cent to 10.5 per cent, that most of these new jobs have been permanent ones, and that the greater increase have been in youth employment. 1 challenge them to prove these figures wrong. It is not enough for them to say they do not believe them, they should quote figures of their own.
Hon. Members opposite claim that only 4 per cent of Canadians will benefit from the capital gains tax exemption. I cannot question this figure, for it is true. But even so, an analysis of Canadian taxpayers who declared capital gains on their Income Tax returns, shows that 55 per cent of them are families earning less than $40,000 a year. These are no millionaires and we are not doing them any favour. First of all, they are not millionaires, for no family earning less than $40,000 a year can be considered rich nowadays. They are just ordinary people. Second, capital gains are not outright gifts, as we keep repeating, they are investment oriented. Yesterday, I quoted a few examples from my own riding, indicating exactly where these job-creating investments would take place.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak on behalf of the elderly in my riding. There are 12 senior citizens' homes in my riding, and residents have asked me to take a message to the Prime Minister. The motion to amend Bill C-51 before the House today asks the Government to reduce its borrowing authority by 3 per cent, because we in the Liberal Party believe that the Government should not apply a double standard. If the elderly must tighten their belts and suffer a 3 per cent cut in pension benefits, it is only fair and equitable that the Government should do the same. For two days I have been watching the situation in the House and listening to speeches, and when I look at the Conservatives opposite, I get the impression that many of them are delighted to see the Opposition fight the battle for them. I think if they were really honest with themselves they would come out and say so. I understand the situation. I had the same thing happen to me when we were in power, and I realize that they may not be in a position at this time to rise in the House to voice their objections. However, their constituents will tell them they are disappointed in their behaviour in the House.
In presenting this motion, the Liberal Party is acting on behalf of thousands of elderly Canadians across the country. This was demonstrated on Parliament Hill today, where we saw Canadian flags from all over the province. They came in large numbers. Since they are not particularly wealthy, Quebec senior citizens all chipped in to rent buses and come to Ottawa to tell the Prime Minister they do not want a cut in their pensions.
I went to meet them. You know what they are afraid of? They are afraid because they think this is only the first of a series of cuts. They told me: This is only the beginning. And believe me, they are right!
Senior citizens have been calling my office in Montreal to protest. They are also calling to congratulate the Liberals and their Members for defending them and their rights. They ask me where to go to sign petitions. Like everyone else, I have received hundreds and hundreds of them. And this is only the beginning. They feel they have been deceived and betrayed by this Government. They are anxious and concerned. They know they cannot afford to cut back any more on what they spend.
I have here a letter from one of my constituents who is single and retired, and who sent me this little budget, a personal budget. I will take the time to read it to you to show the kind of impact that a 3 per cent cut can have on the budget of a single individual.
Income including pension benefits and supplement totals $606.20. Expenses: rent is $240. Hydro: $21.47. Heating: $57. All this is monthly. Telephone: $17. Life insurance and insurance against fire and theft: $20.83. Water taxes: $5. Monthly food bill: $216.50. This adds up to $577.80, leaving $27.40 per month.
This single person has exactly $27.40 to pay for the following: clothing, any medical drugs that are not covered by the card, dental care, glasses, cigarettes, house cleaning supplies, appliance repairs, transportation, newspapers, recreation and personal care (toothpaste, soap, hairdresser, cosmetics, and so forth). Twenty-seven dollars and forty cents a month to pay for all that!
On page 84 of the Budget Papers, under Item 6, the following terms were used to announce that the Budget is increasing the price of personal care products by 11 per cent. It says, and I quote:
The exemption from sales tax applying to a range of consumer goods is being ended, effective July 1, 1985.
This government has re-examined a number of these tax exemptions, as has the Ministerial Task Force on Program Review (headed by the Deputy Prime Minister) which has recommended a repeal of several of them. These exemptions have resulted in a significant erosion of the federal sales tax base.
June 19, 1985

In response to these concerns and to spread the burden of deficit reduction over a wider range of consumer goods, the budget proposes the repeal of the federal sales tax exemption for the following: candy and confectionery; pet food; soft drinks, including carbonated beverages, non-carbonated fruit-flavoured beverages containing less than 25 per cent natural fruit juice, and concentrates for making such beverages; health goods such as medicated creams, lotions, shampoos, soaps, and bandages.
This is a hidden tax, Mr. Chairman, because it is applicable at the manufacturer and group level. But again I say that for a retired person living alone, with the kind of budget I have just described and who has only $27.40 a month to pay for clothing, transportation, shampoo, soap and what have you, it is catastrophic. We Liberals have been accused of spreading fear among senior citizens. We in the Opposition did not spread fear, it is page 16 of the Budget which has created such anxiety among elderly Canadians. It is a bad decision and an error in judgment on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), it is a political error on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Government ought to admit its mistake and should have the courage to reconsider its decision.

I have here a letter dated June 7 which came to my office in the morning mail today. It is from the Federation of New Brunswick Senior Citizens which met in New Brunswick on May 27 and 28. This is what the letter has to say:
The following statement was announced Tuesday in Moncton at a Media Conference by the President: "N.B. Senior Citizens have once again been disturbed in their quality of life. Their internal peace and tranquility is most important at this stage of their lives."
The recent announcements violate a sacred trust, and to Canadian Seniors many things and principles are still sacred.
Tampering with old age security (already inadequate) is immoral, indecent and dishonest.
You can consider this letter as coming from the 76,500 N.B. residents aged 65 and over, seventy-three percent of them below the poverty level, eighty percent of these single ladies and or widows.
Yes we are for measures for reducing deficits-Yes we have paid all of our lives-Yes we are still paying like everyone else-Yes we want a strong Canada-very very few of you are listening to what Senior Citizens are saying. At this time enough is enough!
Fifty-eight percent of Canada's Seniors are below the poverty level. That is a National disgrace!
We will not allow you to legislate our peace of mind, quality of life and the eroding of our mental and physical health under the guise of saving a few dollars.
The letter is signed by Mrs. Edna Bourque, President, and Mr. Bernard Richard, Executive Director.

Mr. Chairman, I have here figures which show the injustice perpetrated on our senior citizens. According to an independent study, over 750,000 Canadian men and women will have fallen under the poverty line by 1990 because of the last Budget. Of all these Canadians, 200,000 will be senior citizens. The Budget of the Progressive Conservative Government contains nothing to improve the situation of the 4.1 Canadians, or 20 per cent of the population, who are already living in unacceptable conditions. On the contrary, the Wilson Budget will increase the financial distress of the poorest members of

our society. The deindexation of old age security pensions will affect senior citizens. By 1990, this will mean a loss of about $1,200 in real income for a couple and $560 a year for someone living alone. What we must remember is that the Government will take away $1.6 million from pensioners before 1990. These figures have human faces, Mr. Chairman. This is why I do not understand why the Government has not decided to reconsider, to reassess the situation and to reinstate full indexation for all senior citizens.
The National Advisory Council on Aging sent me a communique requesting the reinstatement of indexation. Here are a few passages from this communique:
"It is the first time we see such conviction and cohesion among older Canadians", write Mrs. Yhetta Gold, Chairman of the National Advisory Council on Aging in a letter adressed to the Honourable Minister of National Health and Welfare. "The Budget of May 23 ... has incited older Canadians to rally to put pressure on the Government and to defend their own interests. Senior citizens are telling the Government: Now listen here!"
Deindexation has not only united older Canadians, but it has brought together many other Canadians, including young people and business groups."
The letter to the Minister of Health also mentions other effects of deindexation. According to the Council, "it is a short-term saving in exchange for a long term loss".
What they say is rather interesting. They continue:
"The stress caused by an increasingly tight budget will have harmful effects-
-on senior citizens.
More and more Canadians will find it difficult to adjust to their physical, mental or social condition, which will then deteriorate. In time, the cost incurred for all kinds of care will limit the savings brought about by deindexation."
Mrs. Gold seems to be talking about the higher cost of health care, which will result from the stress caused by the reduced purchasing power of our senior citizens.
The National Advisory Council on Aging also believes that people on the eve of retirement, those aged from 60 to 64, of whom there are 1.1 million in Canada, whose income is lower than $17,000 a year will be badly hit by deindexation. "A great number will have to change their retirement plans and try to save more to compensate for their loss of income, or else they will have to postpone their retirement. The first option will reduce economic growth and the second will increase competition on the labour market."
The communique concludes as follows:
Let us not forget that older Canadians, in addition to their political influence and their strength at the polls, also have a substantial purchasing power.
The Government had a social contract with Canadian pensioners and this contract has been broken. During the election campaign, the Government had promised to provide more protection against inflation for pensions. This promise has also been broken. Senior citizens could not believe that the Government would reduce their pensions. They were expecting instead additional protection. I repeat that the Government had promised to provide more protection against inflation for pensions. The reason why my colleague was thrown out of the House this afternoon goes to prove the quotation I just made; every-

thing goes to prove why my colleague was expelled this afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, full inflation protection that is basic to every pension plan: a pension that is reasonable at age 65 becomes inadequate at age 75 if that protection against inflation is not guaranteed.
The poor are asked to tighten their belts in order to make a $5.6 billion gift to the affluent. This budget is unfair to the poor. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that he kept his mind open on the budget, and that he would be willing to make changes if needed.
On behalf of the senior citizens and the poor, Mr. Chairman, I ask him not to delay his decision. Every day counts for our seniors. They are all anxious, they are going to fight to the finish.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is my duty to point out some inaccuracies that crept up hopefully by mistake. Earlier, it was suggested that a person living alone wouuld lose, and I said "would lose", I am quoting in order not to be myself quoted out of context, "would lose" $560 a year. Therefore, if that is the kind of statement that is made to the public at large, it comes as no surprise that they should be anxious. I would therefore like to put the record straight about those $560: this would be an overall amount over the forthcoming five years, under all the provisions that are of course already referred to in the budget.
Second, on these cuts, again that term should not be used the way it is being used by Opposition Members. There is no cut. Nobody is losing money with that. Understand? People will still be increased until December 31, and after December 31 we have options which are very well outlined in the budget. So there is no cut.
Second, when there is reference to, rhetoric, semantics like "reverse", "backtrack", "recognize the error", all that points to the basic goal of this debate. It is purely of a political nature, and it is a shame that senior citizens, should be used, while taking advantage not of their credulity but of their sensitivity, to such vile purposes as the political aims as are now pursued.
I do not believe they have had the honesty to tell senior citizens that everything is provided for in the budget in order that, when the Government feels it is in a position to help them without digging into the old earnings, as I have been told in my constituency, when it becomes sure that the cheque we will then be giving them will not bounce, as hinted today by the Prime Minister, the whole measure will be reviewed. And as the economic situation evolves, as the measures we have been taking to create more wealth produce their benefits, as job creation becomes obvious, as order is restored in the affairs of the state, and as the national debt is checked and the deficit controlled in the first place.
Second, I would also like to put the record straight on the matter of deindexing. There has been references to some promises we made, suggestions that we promised protection. This is basically what we promised, and this is basically what has been achieved. Referring to the budget speech itself, or rather the document that goes with it, it is clearly stated, and I quote: "Recipients of these transfers will be protected from rapid increases in inflation but will no longer receive compensation for inflation as measured by the CPI below 3 per cent a year." etc.
This is on Page 14 of the document The Fiscal Plan.
In effect, this is protection. The difference between the protection we are offering and the protection that was offered by the previous government is this: the present government, or rather the previous government had established a floor, saying we will protect you from 6 per cent and up to 100 per cent, and senior citizens were to make do with that. We, on the other hand, are establishing a ceiling, that is, up to 3 per cent, senior citizens are asked to contribute. Above 3 per cent, the government will step in. I believe that this will enable older people to do some long term planning, sparing them the fear of having to face spiralling inflation such as we have experienced in recent years. I believe they will be spared the fear of having their income eroded by this evil of modern society which is called inflation.
Obviously, I deeply regret the statement that was made a moment ago by the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens) when she mentioned and tried to ennoble the sad incident that happened today during question period. 1 am sorry to say that the person who was expelled from the House deserved it, and I regret even more deeply to see such a behaviour being supported by a party for which 1 once had some respect. That party was badly shaken today. I was the first today to applaud when someone withdrew a statement. In my view, an honest person is not one who never makes any mistakes but one who know how to correct them. So I must say that the hon. member disappointed me in that regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure in this debate to follow my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic, and expand on her very fine presentation. I will start by first dealing with the rather skillful intervention by the Parliamentary Secretary on the government side who, despite his attempt to discredit the credibility of my colleague, cannot deny that we are talking here about a Budget. That is a document which spells very clearly the intention of the Government to deindex pensions above 3 per cent.
A Budget is not, as the Parliamentary Secretary would like us to believe, a White Paper, something which says we "might" do certain things or we may not. The Budget spells out its intentions and its will by the use of words such as "we will" deindex. Therefore, the Parliamentary Secretary fails in his intervention to establish credibility. He fails to deal with the fact that the fear of deindexation has been introduced by the words of the Budget. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept his criticism of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic, because she quite rightly was speaking on what is written in the Budget. The Parliamentary Secretary cannot wipe out her words by stating that the Government "may" do certain things during the next few months, until the words of the Budget are modified.
I am very honoured to take part following the fine speech by my colleague, because for me as well it is important to speak on behalf of the senior citizens in my riding. In the last few days I have seen the spontaneous arrival of petitions to my office in a surge the like of which I have not seen in the last 17 years. It is a new experience for me. It tells me that our amendment today reflects a profound sense of preoccupation based on fear with respect to the proposed deindexation in the Budget of this Tory Government. We are proposing with our amendment a certain measure because we want to put pressure on the Government. We want to bring this Government to its senses and we want to make sure that the Government, as a result of the efforts of the Official Opposition, understands that there is a widespread preoccupation with deindexation in the country. By our amendment, we are speaking on behalf of the senior citizens of Canada in every riding.
I could not believe my ears when in the last few days I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare using the argument that deindexation is intended to create jobs. That linkage, Mr. Chairman, is absurd, and it is understandable that senior citizens in the country have started to come forward to stress this absurdity. It is not by diminishing the purchasing power of pensioners, or by threatening to do so at the beginning of January next year, that you create jobs.
There is a contradiction on the part of the Government itself when it proudly states in the House that in the month of May it has created so many jobs-.55 per cent of the labour force. We are glad to hear that jobs are being created, but in the corresponding month of May, 1984, jobs were created at the rate of .5 per cent instead of .55 per cent of the labour force. Therefore, it is incredible that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would have us believe that the proposed deindex-
Borrowing Authority Act
ation will be a means which will achieve job creation. That is absolutely absurd and almost counterproductive. No one in his or her right mind would buy that argument.
There is another red herring which is coming up in debate, and in Question Period in particular. That is, the Prime Minister and others are saying they will monitor the situation between now and the end of the year to see whether or not this will become a reality. Keep in mind that the measure in the Budget says it "will" become a reality. The word "will" in English is used, not "may", and that is important to remember. I ask you, what will you monitor in the next six months since, by your own text, the measure will come into effect on January 1, 1986? What is there to monitor, or is that a code word for conducting Gallup polls?
Perhaps this notion of monitoring is another way of saying "we will reconsider". Well then, we on this side of the House, and 1 am sure many back-benchers on the other side, wonder why it is necessary to keep the seniors in a state of anxiety for six months. Why not accept the fact that a mistake was made in the Budget? Why not pursue the matter to the ultimate conclusion and announce any day before the end of this month the decision that this idea of deindexation is going to be removed once and for all?
There are good reasons for doing that. You do not reduce the purchasing power of senior citizens because that means you weaken their economic condition at a time when, if anything, they need to be strengthened. You reduce the money going into the economy, you reduce retail sales, and basically and fundamentally you weaken the social security thrust which has been developed in this country over the last few decades and given Canada one of the most outstanding security systems in the world. If you do anything, you build on it. You strengthen it.
I was very impressed by what we were told this morning by senior citizens who came to the Liberal caucus to speak to us. They made the point that they should not be penalized because they are over the age of 65 and did not have the opportunity to receive an income based on a full-time activity. They should not be penalized because there were perceived as perhaps being politically disorganized. Why should they all of a sudden be asked in the name of an absurd notion of creating jobs to accept an erosion of their income of 3 per cent per year, because that is what deindexation is all about.
Over the next five years that will mean the average senior in your riding and mine, Mr. Chairman, will lose several hundred dollars of purchasing power. I ask you, is that the yardstick by which the Progressive Conservative Government of Canada wants to be measured? Evidently it is not, otherwise we would not have a picture of discomfort on the faces of PC backbenchers during Question Period each day.

I am talking about those who have. I am not suggesting that they have all left. Weakness is when you hold on to something which you have long since believed is no longer appropriate. It is weakness when one looks at the facts and circumstances, clearly seeing the conclusion, but failing to accept it. The Government must recognize the difference.
This is a new Government and I can well understand that it does not have the experience of many long years of fighting. I say with great respect that it has not developed the necessary skills to be able to back away. The Prime Minister has taken some steps to move away from this unacceptable policy of partially deindexing the pensions for retired Canadians. He said that the Government has changed it from a policy to a position to be considered, monitored, analysed and ultimately changed. The Government has yet to come to the point of determining how and when this change should take place.
Some of my colleagues in this Party and others in the House have made what I believe is a reasonable analysis of the impact of this measure. We have also made an analysis of the financial impact of the deindexing provision. I am prepared to concede that our analysis is open to question, as are all analyses. However, our analysis of the financial impact is as good and supportable as any other at this point.
The one thing that we know for sure is that if inflation continues-there is no reason to doubt that it will not- pensioners will fall behind in their purchasing power. Let me suggest that the Government would do well to listen rather than talk. It has indicated from the start of its mandate that it will be a consultative Government. Let me suggest to Members who care to listen that consultation is a two-way street. It is not simply meeting with someone so you can tell them the realities. It is letting them explain their view of a problem and then coming to a consensus on the issue. That two-way consultative process continues to be lacking in this issue.
I believe it was a White Paper published by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which the Government determined that there was no need to consult on the matter of pensions because the Government did not intend to change it. With that in mind, it is clear that the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Prime Minister himself did not embark on any discussion of the necessity for or desirability of change.
That is not only the position stated in the White Paper by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It was clearly the position of the Department of Health, as stated by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister when he travelled to Toronto, I believe, in April to meet with a group of seniors when he indicated that there would be no change in the old age pension. Therefore, those who represent the pensioners did not feel the urge or the necessity to indulge in any discussion about indexing or the basic pension that was then available to pensioners.
In those circumstances, it was a shock to pensioners- particularly those who were at the meeting-to discover that the Government had changed its mind without even giving them a hint, asking for their reaction or suggesting to them that their view would be appreciated. Within one month of assuring that no change would take place, the Government simply changed its mind. Is it any wonder that seniors are angry? Is it any wonder that they are confused and do not quite know whether they can trust those who speak on behalf of the Conservative Government?
I say to the Government that on statistical grounds alone, with a financial base as the bottom line, it is not unreasonable to suggest that we can afford to index pensions as they have been indexed in the past. On numerous occasions our Party has offered ways to raise the necessary capital to offset what would be lost by continuing the indexing provision.

From a purely financial point of view, I do not think it is unreasonable to believe that we can afford to index pensions for senior citizens in Canada. When Mulroney launched his assault on the elderly, he struck an exposed Canadian nerve; Canadians from all walks of life have coalesced around the elderly, and in their outrage they have temporarily overlooked the rest of the budget's inadequacies.
Had the Mulroney budget not taken aim at the elderly, more Canadians would be asking how massive new tax hikes are going to foster job creation and increased economic growth. They would be questioning how a $2 billion cut in transfer payments to the provinces is going to promote better education and training for Canada's youth. The Mulroney budget is not a blueprint for tomorrow. It is a leap of faith to the right. If full indexation for the elderly were restored without delay, we might see the broader debate that the budget deserves.
This Prime Minister and government were elected on the promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs". The budget needs to be measured against that promise to 1.3 million unemployed Canadians.

It is not for me to call government Members names. It is not for me to say that they have been uttering terminological inexactitudes. They have been condemned by their own actions as compared to their own promises.
What is a promise? What is a commitment? Is it any wonder that young people across the country think so poorly of politicians? Is it any wonder that the credibility of politicians has been undermined by the actions of so-called responsible individuals who have presented themselves before Parliament? How can they break trust on such fundamental promises as those that were made during the election campaign?
I have received letters from groups representing senior citizens and I want to read some of them for the record. The senior citizens of the community of Skead wrote me a letter, a copy of which was sent to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. The letter reads as follows:
Honourable Sir,
The motion passed at an Emergency Meeting of the Skead Senior Citizens Club is quite plain. The "Seniors" would like to make it clear that our time of restraint has been a continuous one, having experienced the rationing of World War I, the depression years and the lean times to bring World War II to an end and the present depression. The budget has hit the wrong end of the spectrum in its projected fairness.
Seniors, although well trained in restraint, rationing have an understanding of your problems, but feel that their share in this regard has been fulfilled.
An early move to delete this part of the budget would be just and fair.

We of the Skead Senior Citizens Club are pleased to be able to present their views to you, Sir, and feel that our position is well founded.

President Skead Senior Citizens Club 2 Silver Birch Cr,
Skead, Ontario POM 2Y0
How could the Government betray the trust that these people put in it? How could it betray the trust of those who have helped to build and make this country the great country it is? There are people in this country who, when they worked, had no pension plan. The great free enterprise system never saw fit to supply pension plans, so many of those workers who are retired today live strictly on the old age pension.

On the subject of poverty, I would like to deal briefly with employment and women. It should be noted that staff cuts in the Public Service will affect mostly the lower salary levels, namely women. With respect to on-the-job training, the Progressive Conservative Government had pledged to support the introduction of effective programs to help women prepare for technological change and new careers. During the election campaign last summer, a combination of tax incentives and grants was considered among other things for that purpose. Now, the Progressive Conservative Government is going to cut back training programs by $78 million this year. This means that about one sixth of the spending cuts of the Progressive Conservative Government will be at the expense of working men and women who need to improve their skills. There is nothing in the Budget to help women face the technological change. Since the Progressive Conservative Government is eager to reduce the Government's involvement in the economy and hand it over to the open market, women will have to fall back on their own resources to adapt to technological change.
With respect to equal employment, the Human Rights Commission had been entrusted with the necessary enforcement measures. Now, with the real cuts in departmental budgets, that is with deindexation, it is more doubtful than ever if the Commission will ever dispose of enough human and financial resources to perform its role, and this, Mr. Speaker, does not include the cuts to be brought in by Mr. Nielsen's group as of September and February next. Employment equity, to say the least, does not seem to be a priority for the Progressive Conservative government, which greatly concerns me for the future.
In this Budget, the Progressive Conservative government has completely ignored part-time workers men and women. Thirty per cent of them would rather hold a full time job. The
June 19, 1985

occurrence of poverty in families where the head of the household works part time is five times greater than in those where the bread-winner works full time.
