It shows total lacks of interest on the part of the Prime Minister towards the specific problems women are up against, in the labour market. Because of a complete lack of strategy on the part of the Government with regard to the labour market, women holding part-time jobs will still have to face a series of problems that seem insignificant to hon. Members opposite, for instance lack of access to social benefits and pensions, a low rate of pay, a high number of women in ghettos, a minimal number of unionized workers, a lack of opportunities for promotion or retraining, no security of employment and inadequate day-care services.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the impact of the Budget on immigration, two things should be remebered, the de-indexation of department funds will mean gradual reduction in the amounts allocated to the immigration program. That was to be expected on the basis of the estimates. The Consultative Council on the Status of Refugees appropriations remain the same, however the funds allocated to the Immigration Appeal Board have been reduced by $2.5 million, inflation factor included. Today, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) introduced a special bill to increase the number of members on the Immigration Appeal Board from 16 to 50. I hope that I will have an opportunity to discuss this bill and explain that the new procedure of reducing the quorum from three to one is unacceptable for refugees.
We have yet to see which changes the government intends to make in the way refugee status is granted. The fact that the immigration program budget will be reduced in real terms is not a good omen, especially since the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration is considering a raise in the immigration level from 90,000 to 200,000 this year. It would seem ridiculous to cut services for immigrants when we are planning to double their number.
The first victims of those cuts will be the immigrants themselves. But in the long run, all Canadian men and women will suffer from this conservative immigration policy. Without the benefit of those services, immigrants will be more vulnerable to economic vagaries and they will be more dependent on welfare and unemployment insurance.
I referred earlier to the bet taken up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) concerning employment as related to immigration. The Conservative Government is taking up another bet, i.e. to offer quality services to immigrants by having them provided by humanitarian organizations and this of course without granting the latter any funds.
That tallies with the Progressive Conservative Government's philosophy: privatize some activities and commit others to outside organizations. Already the lease the Government had signed with the Avion Hotel in Toronto for people claiming
Borrowing Authority Act
refugee status has been brought to an end. The Government expects charitable organizations to provide services to immigrants. When we know that in times of economic recession those organizations have to cope with reduced funds, we realize that the Progressive Conservative Government intends to have the quality of services to immigrants subjected to economic circumstances. It is a mean thing to do, to say the least. This is another way to penalize the neediest for the sake of deficit reduction.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I want to point out that whenever budget cuts are being dealt with, the Progressive Conservative Government equates them with increased government efficiency. For instance, the Government will state that in order to improve the efficiency of its manpower adjustment programs, it has decided in 1985-86 to cut by $78 million the funds allotted for General Industrial Training and for Critical Trade Skills Training. However, management efficiency has no relation whatsoever with the decrease or increase in program costs. A better management efficiency simply means a different work organization, or improved working methods.
So I call upon the Government to tell Canadian men and women about its new magical management methods for improving government efficiency with less money. If they do not tell them, people will simply fear, and rightly so, a reduction of services combined with a reduction of costs.

Mr. Chairman, that is precisely the point 1 was making but if the Hon. Member fails to recognize that those $18.2 billion are part of transfer payments to the provinces, if he does not pay enough attention to what is being said in this place to realize that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation falls under government's jurisdiction, I cannot accept his judgment.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to excuse the Hon. Member since I referred only to the main elements of those $18.2 billion and to the amendment. Why do we want to cut the government borrowing authority by 3 per cent? Because it has been so insensitive to the plea of older people that it did not realize what a 3 per cent reduction meant for them. So, we thought we could make the government aware of the importance of such a reduction if it had itself to do with revenues cut by 3 per cent until the end of the year. The amendment would force the government to reflect on the situation older people will go through once they have paid their housing, food and other bills. I hope the Hon. Member will think about it before he goes to bed tonight, that he will reflect upon the impact of a 3 per cent cut for a widow or an older citizen who lives in an apartment or a home with only $27 left for personal expenses at the end of the month. If the Hon. Member finds such action too complicated, I suggest he speak to his neighbours who live on old age pension and he will know what a 3 per cent cut means.
Unfortunately, the Hon. Member is the living example of the government opposite, Mr. Chairman. They do not know what a 3 per cent reduction means for some people when it is often the difference between luxury and basic essentials. I know a lady from Baie-Comeau who told me that she had to travel by taxi to Haute-Rive twice a month at $12 a trip. That means she has to pay $24 each month to get medical care and if the government goes ahead with this bill, she might be forced to cancel her treatment. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will feel responsible every time an older person goes to the grocery store to buy the cheapest stale bread because it never occurred to him that his own parents could have lived through that sort of hardship. If that is his way of showing his appreciation for the work of our seniors, Mr. Speaker, I will not have it. I do not accept that our senior citizens, who have built this country, be treated in such a way, and if the Government hopes to convince Members from this side of the House to cut the income of senior citizens, and to make us believe this is right, it is mistaken. Senior citizens and average Canadians will not accept that.
